what_it_does: Multiplying two sparse matrices — matrices where most entries are zero, which is common in graph algorithms and certain AI models — is called SpGEMM (sparse-sparse matrix multiplication). The most efficient way to organize this computation (the 'dataflow': whether to sweep row-by-row, column-by-column, or dot-product style) depends heavily on the specific pattern of non-zero entries in the input matrices, and no single ordering wins across all patterns. Hardware accelerators that support multiple dataflows carry extra circuitry that goes unused most of the time. Misam tackles both problems: a small decision-tree classifier (a fast, interpretable model that asks a series of yes/no questions about the matrix's non-zero statistics) picks the best dataflow configuration at runtime for a given input. Because the system runs on an FPGA (a chip whose internal wiring can be reprogrammed in software), it can load a different, highly specialized hardware layout (bitstream) tailored to whichever dataflow was chosen, so no resources are wasted supporting unused configurations — though this reconfiguration itself takes time, and the system only switches when the expected benefit outweighs that cost.
